content: Estradiol topical increases the risk of developing endometrial cancer, which is cancer of the uterine lining. The longer you use estradiol, the higher the risk of developing this type of cancer. If you have not had a hysterectomy (surgical removal of the uterus), your doctor should prescribe a progestin to be taken alongside topical estradiol. This combination may reduce the risk of endometrial cancer but could increase the risk of other health issues, such as breast cancer. Before starting topical estradiol, inform your doctor if you have or have ever had cancer or if you experience abnormal or unusual vaginal bleeding. If you notice abnormal or unusual vaginal bleeding during treatment, contact your doctor immediately. Your doctor will monitor you closely to ensure you do not develop endometrial cancer during or after treatment. Studies have shown that women who take oral estrogens (including estradiol) with progestins have a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, blood clots in the lungs or legs, breast cancer, and dementia (loss of cognitive abilities). Women using topical estradiol alone or with progestins may also face an increased risk of these conditions. Inform your doctor if you smoke, have had a heart attack or stroke in the past year, or if you or a family member has a history of blood clots or breast cancer. Additionally, let your doctor know if you have or have ever had high blood pressure, high cholesterol or fat levels, diabetes, heart disease, lupus, breast lumps, or an abnormal mammogram. Be vigilant for symptoms that may indicate serious health conditions, such as sudden severe headaches, severe vomiting, speech problems, dizziness, fainting, sudden vision loss, double vision, weakness or numbness in an arm or leg, crushing chest pain, coughing up blood, sudden shortness of breath, breast lumps or changes, nipple discharge, difficulty thinking clearly, memory problems, or pain, tenderness, or redness in one leg. If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your doctor immediately. To minimize risks, do not use topical estradiol alone or with progestins to prevent heart disease, heart attacks, or strokes. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary to control your symptoms. Discuss with your doctor every 3–6 months whether you should lower your dose or discontinue the medication. Perform monthly breast self-exams and have an annual mammogram and breast exam by a doctor to detect breast cancer early. Your doctor may recommend more frequent exams based on your personal or family medical history. If you are scheduled for surgery or will be on bed rest, inform your doctor. They may advise you to stop using topical estradiol 4–6 weeks before surgery or bed rest to reduce the risk of blood clots. Regularly discuss the risks and benefits of using topical estradiol with your doctor. Estradiol topical gel and emulsion are used to treat and prevent hot flashes in menopausal women. The gel is also used to treat vaginal dryness, itching, and burning associated with menopause. Women with only vaginal symptoms may benefit more from a medication applied directly to the vagina. Estradiol belongs to a class of medications called estrogen hormones and works by replacing estrogen that the body no longer produces. Topical estradiol is available as a gel or emulsion to be applied to the skin, usually once daily. The emulsion should be applied in the morning, while the gel can be applied at any time of day but should be applied at the same time each day. Follow your prescription instructions carefully and do not use more or less than prescribed. Apply the gel in a thin layer to one arm, from wrist to shoulder, or the emulsion to both thighs and calves. Do not apply estradiol to your breasts. Ensure the application area is clean, dry, and free of irritation. If you bathe, shower, or use a sauna, apply the medication afterward. Allow time between applying the gel and activities like swimming or applying sunscreen. Avoid smoking or being near open flames until the gel dries, as it is flammable. If the gel gets into your eyes, rinse with warm water and contact a doctor if irritation occurs. To use estradiol gel, prime the pump by pressing it down twice and discarding the gel that comes out. Do not repeat this step after the first use. Dispense one dose onto your palm and spread it thinly over your arm. Do not rub or massage the gel into your skin. Allow the skin to dry for 5 minutes before covering it with clothing. Wash your hands with soap and water after application. For the emulsion, open a pouch, apply its contents to one thigh, and rub it into the entire thigh and calf for 3 minutes until absorbed. Rub any remaining emulsion on your hands onto your buttocks. Repeat with a second pouch for the other thigh and calf. Wait until the skin is dry before covering it with clothing. Wash your hands after application. Before using topical estradiol, inform your doctor if you are allergic to estradiol or any of its ingredients, or if you are taking any other medications, vitamins, or supplements. Certain medications may interact with estradiol, so your doctor may need to adjust your doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had asthma, seizures, migraines, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, jaundice, abnormal calcium levels, porphyria, or gallbladder, thyroid, liver, pancreas, or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. Avoid unnecessary sun exposure and use protective clothing and sunscreen, as estradiol may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Do not let others touch the application site for at least one hour after applying the medication, as it may harm others, especially men and children. If you miss a dose of estradiol gel and remember more than 12 hours before your next dose, apply it immediately. If less than 12 hours remain, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not apply extra gel to make up for a missed dose. If you miss a dose of estradiol emulsion, apply it as soon as you remember, but do not apply it more than once daily. Topical estradiol may cause minor side effects, such as headaches, breast pain, upset stomach, diarrhea, constipation, gas, heartburn, weight changes, mood changes, depression, nervousness, sleep disturbances, changes in sexual desire, back pain, runny nose, cough, flu-like symptoms, hair loss, unwanted hair growth, skin darkening, difficulty wearing contact lenses, or skin irritation at the application site. Inform your doctor if these symptoms persist or worsen. Serious side effects include bulging eyes, yellowing of the skin or eyes, itching, loss of appetite, fever, joint pain, stomach pain or swelling, uncontrollable movements, hives, skin rash or blisters, swelling of the face or extremities, hoarseness, wheezing, or difficulty breathing or swallowing. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Topical estradiol may increase the risk of ovarian cancer and gallbladder disease requiring surgery. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Store topical estradiol in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture, and do not freeze it. Discard outdated or unused medication properly. Dispose of the gel pump after 64 doses, even if it is not empty. Consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the victim collapses or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose may include upset stomach, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for monitoring. Inform laboratory personnel that you are using topical estradiol before any tests. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist for questions about refilling your prescription.
